title: Peel a Tree Leaf Layer by Layer
statement:
You peel a binary tree in rounds. In each round you remove all of the current leaves (nodes with no children) at once and write down their values. Removing them may turn their parents into leaves for the next round. You stop when the tree is empty.

Return the list of rounds. Inside each round, list the values from left to right as the nodes appear in the tree.

Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child.

examples.why: 9 is not peeled in the second round together with 4: it still has the child 4 then. A node's round is its height, not its depth.
The root alone is a leaf and goes in the first round.
Values can repeat; collect them by position, not by value.

constraints: The tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: Simulating the rounds works, but every round rescans the tree. Can you tell in which round a node is removed without simulating?
A leaf goes in round 0. A node goes one round after the later of its two children. That is the node's height: the number of edges on the longest path down to a leaf.
One post-order DFS: compute height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)), with height(null) = −1, and append the value to layers[height]. Post-order visits same-height nodes left to right.

explain.intuition:
A node becomes a leaf once both of its subtrees are gone. Its children disappear in their own rounds, so the node goes in the round right after the later of the two. Leaves are round 0, so the round number is exactly the node's height, the length of the longest path from it down to a leaf. Depth (distance from the root) is the wrong measure, which the first example shows.

Heights come from a single post-order walk, children before parent: h = 1 + max(h(left), h(right)), with an empty child counting as −1. Push each value into layers[h] as you return. Two nodes with the same height can never be ancestor and descendant, so post-order meets them in left-to-right order, which is the order the problem asks for.
steps: If layers has no entry h yet, add one. Push node.val into layers[h] and return h.
pitfalls: Grouping by depth from the root instead of by height. In the first example 9 and 4 have different heights.
Using the minimum child height instead of the maximum. A node stays as long as its deepest subtree.
Using a pre-order walk, which records a node before knowing its height.

solutions.title: Simulate the rounds
solutions.idea: Each round, walk the tree, collect the current leaves left to right and cut them off. Repeat until the root itself is removed.

solutions.title: Group nodes by height in one DFS
solutions.idea: The round a node is removed in equals its height. A post-order walk computes heights bottom-up and drops each value into its bucket.

followups: Do it without recursion. What extra state does the explicit stack need?
